subject: Career
title: The Contrast Effect Between Candidates
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Contrast Effect Between Candidates.

hook.text: A mediocre candidate after three terrible ones looks brilliant. Context distorts judgment.

buildup.text: The contrast effect means we judge things relative to what came before, not on absolute merit.

discovery.text: Your interview slot matters more than you think. After a strong candidate, you look weaker.

twist.text: You can't control your slot, but you can control your anchor — start with your strongest story.

climax.text: Scorecards help interviewers evaluate against the role, not against the last person.

punchline.text: You're not competing with candidates. You're competing with their memory.

quiz.question: What is the contrast effect in interviewing?
options: Judging candidates relative to who came before

details.summary: The contrast effect causes interviewers to evaluate candidates relative to the person interviewed just before them rather than against objective criteria. A mediocre candidate looks great after a weak one, and vice versa.
details.whyItMatters: Your interview performance is partly judged by who happened to go before you. Understanding this bias helps you focus on delivering a standout absolute performance rather than worrying about competitors.
takeaways: Interview order can shift ratings by up to fifteen percent
Morning slots often receive slightly higher average ratings
Structured scorecards reduce but do not eliminate contrast effects

faq.question: Does it matter what time slot you choose for an interview?
faq.answer: Early morning or immediately after lunch tend to yield slightly more favorable evaluations because interviewers are fresher. Late afternoon candidates often face tired, less engaged interviewers. Request an early slot when given the choice.

faq.question: Can the contrast effect work in your favor as a candidate?
faq.answer: If the previous candidate performed poorly, you benefit. However, since you cannot control this, the best strategy is to deliver consistently strong, evidence-based answers that stand on their own regardless of the comparison context.
